## Hosea 11: Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — "When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son."

**Traditional Reading**

- God looks back to Israel's national infancy — the Egyptian bondage and Exodus — recalling His fatherly love for the nation. "Youth" pictures the infancy of Israel as a nation before it was established in Canaan. God's love was sovereign and antecedent to any Israelite merit (Dt 7:7–8). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-11-commentary)
- The phrase "My son" unmistakably refers to national Israel, drawn from Exodus 4:22 ("Israel is My son, My firstborn"). The Exodus was the loving Father redeeming His son from slavery. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-11-commentary)
- This verse sets the tone for the whole chapter: it is not merely the story of a rebellious nation breaking laws, but of a beloved son breaking his Father's heart. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-11-commentary)

**Matthew 2:15 and Christ**

- Matthew 2:15 quotes this verse as "fulfilled" when the infant Jesus returned from Egypt. Hosea's original context looks backward to the Exodus, not forward as a prediction. Matthew, under inspiration, sees Israel's history recapitulated and brought to its fullest expression in Jesus Christ — Jesus is the true and ideal Israel. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-11-commentary)
- Ellicott: "In this context there cannot be a prophecy of the Christ, for obstinate conduct and rebellion would thus be involved in the prediction." The calling out of Egypt of the Messiah gave a new indication of the cyclical character of Hebrew history. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/11.htm)
- David Guzik (Enduring Word): This is an "unexpected" prophecy fulfilled in the life of Jesus — Matthew shows how the words were fulfilled when the child Jesus returned from Egypt. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-11/)

**Denominational Distinctive: Baptist (Gill)**

- John Gill argues the words refer "not to literal Israel… but his own natural and only begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ; for these words are expressly said to be fulfilled in him, Matthew 2:15; not by way of allusion… but literally: the first and only sense of the words respects Christ." The calling of literal Israel out of Egypt was only a type. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/11.htm)

---

### v. 2 — "But the more I called Israel, the farther they departed from Me. They sacrificed to the Baals and burned incense to carved images."

**Traditional Reading**

- God called Israel through His prophets, but the more He called, the further they went. The prophets called them to the worship and service of God, but "they turned a deaf ear to them, and their backs upon them." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/11.htm)
- Ellicott: "As they (i.e., the prophets) called them, so they (Israel) went from them — sought to avoid the voice and presence of the men of God." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/11.htm)
- David Guzik: God called Israel out of Egypt, but the idolatry of the Baals called to Israel, and they forsook the LORD and followed the local deities of Canaan. The tragic contrast is that Israel was called by God and called by the Baals — and answered the wrong call. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-11/)
- Gill notes an alternative interpretation by Aben Ezra: it was the false prophets who called them to idolatry, and they went after them. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/11.htm)

---

### v. 3 — "It was I who taught Ephraim to walk, taking them in My arms, but they never realized that it was I who healed them."

**Traditional Reading**

- The picture is of a parent teaching a child to walk by holding the child's arms and supporting them through their awkward steps. God personally cared for Israel, supported them, and protected them when they stumbled. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-11-commentary)
- Gill: The allusion is to a mother or nurse stooping down, setting the child on its feet, forming its steps, teaching it how to go — and also bearing and carrying them in His arms as a father carries his son (Dt 1:31). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/11.htm)
- "They did not know that I healed them": God does so much for His people that they are unaware of, often attributing blessings to some other source. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-11/)
- Ellicott draws a modern parallel: "This obtuseness to the source of all mercies — the refusal to recognise the true origin in Divine revelation of those ideas which… are treated as 'the voice of nature,' or 'development of humanity'… is one of the commonest and most deadly sins of modern Christendom." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/11.htm)

---

### v. 4 — "I led them with cords of kindness, with ropes of love; I lifted the yoke from their necks and bent down to feed them."

**Traditional Reading**

- **"Cords of a man / cords of kindness"**: God drew Israel not with the cords used to restrain unmanageable beasts but with cords suited to human beings — in a rational, gentle, kind, loving, and fatherly manner. He does not coerce; He draws with love. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/11.htm)
- Ellicott: "Cords of a man — in contrast with the cords with which unmanageable beasts are held in check. Israel is led with 'bands of love,' not of compulsion." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/11.htm)
- Adam Clarke (cited by Guzik): "This is a reference to leading strings, one end of which is held by the child, the other by the nurse, by which the little one, feeling some support, and gaining confidence, endeavours to walk." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-11/)
- **"I lifted the yoke from their necks"**: As one who is merciful to his beast — a kind husbandman who takes off the yoke so the animal can rest and feed freely. This refers to Israel's deliverance from Egyptian bondage. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/11.htm)
- **"I bent down to feed them"**: God humbled Himself to minister to His needy people — the heart reflected in the servant nature of Jesus (Philippians 2). Ellicott renders it: "And gently towards them gave I food to eat, expressing the tenderness, delicacy, and condescension of his personal regard." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/11.htm), (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-11/)

**Baptist (Spurgeon)**

- Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik): "Understand, then, it is true that no man comes to God except he is drawn; but it is equally true that God draweth no man contrary to the constitution of man, but his methods of drawing are in strict accordance with ordinary mental operations. He finds the human mind what it is, and he acts upon it, not as upon matter, but as upon mind. The compulsions, the constraints, the cords that he uses, are 'cords of a man.' The bands he employs are 'bands of love.'" This balances divine sovereignty in drawing with human responsiveness. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-11/)

---

### v. 5 — "Will they not return to the land of Egypt and be ruled by Assyria because they refused to repent?"

**Traditional Reading**

- Though the BSB renders it as a question, the traditional sense (KJV, NASB) is declarative: "He shall not return to the land of Egypt; but the Assyrian shall be his king." Israel will go into a bondage worse than Egypt — captivity under Assyria. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/11.htm)
- Ellicott prefers to read both clauses as interrogative (with Ewald): "Shall he not return into the land of Egypt? And shall not the Assyrian be his king?" — rhetorical questions affirming the coming judgment. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/11.htm)
- The root cause is singled out: "because they refused to repent." It was not so much the sin itself, but the stubborn refusal to repent after sinning, that brought destruction and exile. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-11/)
- Gill: They "refused to return" — to the Lord from whom they had backslidden, and to His pure worship, word, and ordinances. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/11.htm)

---

### v. 6 — "A sword will flash through their cities; it will destroy the bars of their gates and consume them in their own plans."

**Traditional Reading**

- The sword of the Assyrians would fall upon and abide on their cities — not just Samaria (besieged three years) but all cities. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/11.htm)
- Ellicott: the English version is incorrect here. The word for "branches" is literally "bars" — meaning the princes, heroes, leaders, or defenders of the state being aptly called barriers or bulwarks. "Then shall the sword be brandished amid his cities, and utterly destroy his princes." The Targum renders it "his mighty men." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/11.htm)
- "Because of their own counsels": their own plans — political alliances with Egypt, idolatrous worship, rejection of God's counsel through the prophets — brought the ruin upon them. God's counsels would have saved them, but their own counsels ruined them. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/11.htm), (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-11/)

---

### v. 7 — "My people are bent on turning from Me. Though they call to the Most High, He will by no means exalt them."

**Traditional Reading**

- "Bent on backsliding": there is a propensity, a bias, a settled inclination toward turning away. They are "bent upon it, and pertinaciously abide in it; nor will they be reclaimed." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/11.htm)
- Ellicott: "No imagery is used… but homely literal commonplace. The people were called by sufficient means to the highest worship, but they were bent on the lowest." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/11.htm)
- David Guzik: Backsliding means at one time Israel had a closer walk with God; now their profession is simply empty. They call to the Most High in a formal sort of way, but they do not exalt Him with their lives. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-11/)
- Gill notes an alternative reading: "my people are in suspense about returning to me" — hesitating, divided, not deciding whether to return or not. The Targum: "my people divide (or hesitate) to return to my law." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/11.htm)

---

### v. 8 — "How could I give you up, O Ephraim? How could I surrender you, O Israel? How could I make you like Admah? How could I treat you like Zeboiim? My heart is turned within Me; My compassion is stirred!"

**Traditional Reading**

- One of the most emotionally powerful passages in all of Hebrew prophecy. The four "How?" questions express extreme reluctance — God cannot bear to treat His people as He treated the cities of the plain. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/11.htm)
- Admah and Zeboiim were cities destroyed alongside Sodom and Gomorrah (Dt 29:23). God says He cannot bear to allow His people to be caught up in that kind of total, irremediable destruction. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-11/)
- Gill sees this as a debate in the divine mind between justice and mercy — justice demanding the delivery of sinners, mercy pleading on their behalf, and mercy getting the victory. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/11.htm)
- Ellicott: "Mine heart is turned within me — Better, against me — a violent revulsion of feeling. Divine compassion pleads with Divine justice." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/11.htm)
- Bridgeway Commentary: "It hurts God to have to punish those whom he loves. He must punish them for their wickedness, because he cannot ignore sin. But within his justice there is mercy. His love is stronger and more faithful than anything that is found in human relationships." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/hosea-11.html)

**Reformed (Ligonier)**

- This passage illustrates the interplay of covenant grace and covenant obedience. Israel had to suffer exile because of faithlessness, yet God remembered His love based on His sovereign choice, not their worthiness. God would not destroy Israel completely and finally like Admah and Zeboiim. This points to God's grace in preserving a remnant. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lords-tender-compassion)

---

### v. 9 — "I will not execute the full fury of My anger; I will not turn back to destroy Ephraim. For I am God and not man— the Holy One among you— and I will not come in wrath."

**Traditional Reading**

- God will leave a remnant and restore the nation rather than wiping Israel out. Judgment is tempered by mercy. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-11/)
- **"For I am God and not man"**: God's forgiveness and compassion are of an entirely different order from human forgiveness. "The longsuffering, forgiveness, and compassion of the Lord toward His people seems unbelievable until we recognize that He is not man, but God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-11/)
- Ellicott: "This sublime passage is remarkable as drawing illustrations from human emotions, and yet repudiating all human weakness." It suggests Divine mercy in its greatness and Divine justice too — both being infinite, they can adjust themselves beyond human experience. "The Holy One in the midst of thee is such a blending of justice and mercy." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/11.htm)
- "I will not come in wrath": Ellicott notes many commentators interpret the Hebrew *b'îr* to mean "in wrath" rather than "into the city," and prefers this reading. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/11.htm)

**Baptist (Spurgeon, via Guzik)**

- Spurgeon drew up a list of contrasts between God's forgiveness and man's: Man cannot hold back anger long; God can. Man will not reconcile if the offender is of bad character; God will. Man often requires the offender to make the first move; God does not. Man does not bear the penalty himself; God did in Christ. Man puts the offender on probation; God restores without conditions. Man will not love, adopt, honor, and associate with one who has wronged him; God does exactly that. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-11/)

---

### v. 10 — "They will walk after the LORD; He will roar like a lion. When He roars, His children will come trembling from the west."

**Traditional Reading**

- A promise of restoration. God will call His people back, and they will respond. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-11/)
- Ellicott renders it: "They shall go up after Jehovah, who roars as a lion; yea, he shall roar so that the children…" The lion imagery recalls lions that accompanied Egyptian monarchs to battle — a picture of power and authority. "West" means the coastlands and islands of the Levant. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/11.htm)
- "Trembling" means coming with awe-stricken joy to the voice of the Divine summons — not terror, but reverent eagerness. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/11.htm)
- Calvin (via search excerpt): "When the Prophet says, that they shall walk after Jehovah, he proceeds farther than before; for here he refers not to the mitigation of punishment, but promises restoration." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/hosea-11.html)

---

### v. 11 — "They will come trembling like birds from Egypt and like doves from the land of Assyria. Then I will settle them in their homes, declares the LORD."

**Traditional Reading**

- God will gather His people from all places of exile — Egypt and Assyria representing the two great powers among whom Israel was scattered. They will come swiftly, like birds. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/11.htm)
- Ellicott: "The prophetic word looks beyond the restoration of the sixth century B.C. to the gathering together of some from east and west, from all the places where they are hidden in exile under the lion of the tribe of Judah; the broader and grander accomplishment will satisfy and more than fulfil the yearnings of the spiritual Israel." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/11.htm)
- Utley: "Many Jews fled Egypt during the Babylonian invasion and exile. God will bring His people home!" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/hosea-11.html)
- Clarke: "They shall have their temple once more, and all their holy ordinances." (From search excerpt — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/hosea-11.html)

---

### v. 12 — "Ephraim surrounds Me with lies, the house of Israel with deceit; but Judah still walks with God and is faithful to the Holy One."

**Traditional Reading (Masoretic/English text)**

- The BSB follows the traditional reading: God acknowledges Israel's (Ephraim's) present encirclement of Him with lies, yet contrasts this with Judah, who "still walks with God." The promises of restoration in vv. 10–11 are made with full knowledge of Israel's present unfaithfulness. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-11/)

**Textual and Translation Issues**

- **Hebrew Bible placement**: This verse stands as the first verse of Hosea 12 in the Hebrew text. Ellicott: "Should stand as the first verse of Hosea 12, just as in the Hebrew text. The rest of the prophecy appears as a distinct composition, a new commencement of judgment and incrimination." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/11.htm)
- **Alternate reading for Judah**: Ellicott notes the English version ("Judah yet ruleth with God") follows Jewish scholars who saw a reference to Hezekiah's reign, but this is "opposed to the mention of the 'controversy with Judah' in Hosea 12:3." Many scholars (Ewald, Wünsche, Nowack) render it: "And Judah still roves unbridled towards God, and towards the faithful Holy One" — meaning Judah too is inconstant, contrasting with God's faithfulness. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/11.htm)
- Utley similarly renders: "Judah is also unruly against God, Even against the Holy One who is faithful" — emphasizing the tension between unconditional covenant (God's character) and conditional covenant (human obedience). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/hosea-11.html)

---

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Perspectives

### Reformed / Presbyterian (Ligonier, Monergism)
- The chapter is read through the lens of **covenant theology**: God's unconditional election and covenant love are set alongside conditional covenant obedience. God preserves a remnant by grace alone. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lords-tender-compassion)
- Monergism's sermon collection emphasizes "the Lord's covenant love… the tension between just judgment and compassionate mercy… steadfast love ultimately preserves a remnant." (https://www.monergism.com/topics/sermon-manuscripts-mp3s-scripture/hosea/audio-multimedia/hosea-%E2%80%94-reformed-sermons-bible-10)

### Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill)
- **Gill**: Holds that Hosea 11:1 points literally and primarily to Christ, not Israel; the Exodus was a type. This is a stronger Christological reading than most traditions. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/11.htm)
- **Spurgeon**: Emphasises that God's drawing ("cords of a man") works *through* human constitution, not against it — a balance between divine sovereignty and human responsiveness. His list of contrasts between divine and human forgiveness (v. 9) is a celebrated distinctive. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-11/)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
- The emphasis is on the **tender, personal, relational heart of God** — His patience, His gentle drawing, His stooping to feed. Application is strongly devotional: "When we receive God's blessings without recognizing them as His work… we miss the point of His patient, gentle love." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-11/)

### Anglican (Ellicott)
- Measured, text-critical, and restrained. Ellicott resists reading v. 1 as a direct Messianic prophecy, notes translation issues (v. 6 "branches" = "princes"; v. 12 belongs to ch. 12 in Hebrew; Judah may be condemned alongside Israel), and sees the fulfillment language in Matthew as typological/cyclical rather than predictive. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/11.htm)
